senses: A light, translucent cotton fabric used for making curtains and dresses.
ety: Borrowed from French voile (“veil”). Doublet of veil and velum.
examples: The domestic voile made from imported gray yarns and woven in the United States is the best combination to be had.
Pull out the basting thread, gently remove the voile from the three-minute sample, and reshape the sample with a steam iron.

senses: A particular thing.
A distinctive characteristic or quality; a peculiarity.
The condition of being particular rather than general or universal; specificity.
Attention to detail; fastidiousness.
ety: From Middle French particularité (“part of a whole; something particular, particularity”) (modern French particularité), and from its etymon Late Latin particularitas (“fact or quality of being particular; something particular, particularity”), from Latin particulāris (“particular; partial”) + -tās (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns indicating a state of being). Particulāris is derived from particula (“particle, small part”) (from pars (“a part, piece, portion, share”) (probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *perh₃- (“to provide, produce, beget”)) + -cula (diminutive suffix)) + -āri
examples: Donny’s obsession for trains is just a harmless particularity of his.

senses: Of or related to the number ten.
Of or related to a decade, in its various senses.
ety: From decade + -al.
examples: About the same time in a decadal sense, there was a rather unexpected discovery.

senses: Contented, pleased, satisfied.
ety: Back-formation from disgruntled.
examples: He spoke with a certain what-is-it in his voice, and I could see that, if not actually disgruntled, he was far from being gruntled.
It had been a rough day, so when I walked into the party I was very chalant, despite my efforts to appear gruntled and consolate.
After all, a number of players were disgruntled, and a few more were gruntled.

senses: Bishops seen as a group.
The tenure in office of a bishop.
ety: From Late Latin episcopatus, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watching over”).
examples: The American Roman Catholic episcopate meets regularly.
Bishop Smith's episcopate ran for more than 30 years.

senses: Awkward, ungainly; lacking grace or dexterity in movement.
Left-handed.
ety: From gawk + -y.
examples: The “gawky” illustrations look as though they may have been done by Belva Jean herself (Bulletin, Mar. 1989).

senses: An ancient Greek and Macedonian military unit that consisted of several ranks and files (lines) of soldiers in close array with joined shields and long spears.
A large group of people, animals or things, compact or closely massed, or tightly knit and united in common purpose.
A Fourierite utopian community; a phalanstery.
ety: Borrowed from Latin phalanx or Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order; array”). Doublet of phalange, planch, plancha, planche, and plank.
examples: Broad phalanx of cars across the bridge moving slowly through the streaming snow.
There, the Paisleyites were being held back by another phalanx of soldiers and policemen.
For a short time the two phalanges of men faced each other at a distance apart.

senses: The capacity to know everything.
ety: From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).
examples: Many people believe in God's omniscience.

senses: A vocal melody or instrumental passage in a smooth, lyrical style.
ety: Borrowed from Italian or Latin cantilēna.
examples: He played a lazy tune that sinuated from C sharp down to G natural and back again. Astonishing that he could flute so lazy a cantilena while chasing nymphs.

senses: A system of doctrines concerning final matters, such as death.
The study of the end times—the end of the world, notably in Christian and Islamic theology, the second coming of Christ, the Apocalypse, or the Last Judgment.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἔσχατος (éskhatos, “last”) + English -logy.
examples: Eschatology and proleptics aside, I think this is a really stupid way to read a mystery novel.

senses: A type of volcanic ash used for mortar or for cement which sets under water.
ety: Borrowed from Italian pozz(u)olana, earth of Pozzuoli, a town near Naples, itself from Latin Puteoli, ultimately from the verb puteō (“stink”).
examples: Finally the street is strewn with pozzolana to prevent the horses from slipping on the smooth paving.

senses: A serving of beer.
ety: From brew + -ski.
examples: Yeah, going for a brewski after a rousing game of touch football with your work team will help you replenish your protein better than a glass of chardonnay.
Budweiser says this will be the first of many excursions it plans to back. And, eventually, the newly gleaned information could inform how the company will make brewskis for Mars.

senses: The Hand of Fatima.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew חַמְסָה (khámsa), from Arabic خَمْسَة (ḵamsa, “five”), used among Jews of Arabic origin for the fingers on the hand.
examples: Reverence for the amulets cuts across religious boundaries. Jews come for Kabbalistic bracelets, glass hamsas or strings of ceramic pomegranates.
Variously associated with qualities ranging from warding off evil to promoting fertility, the open hand of the hamsa is thought to have originated in Mesopotamia and is recognized the world over.

senses: To do without (something enjoyable); to relinquish.
To refrain from, to abstain from.
ety: From Middle English forgon (“to go by, pass up”), from Old English forgān (“to go away, forgo”); equivalent to for- + go.
examples: I've had to forgo my student discount in exchange for taking the job.
But, what afflicts my peace with keenest ruth, / Is, that I have my inner self abused, / Forgone the home delight of constant truth, / And clear and open soul, so prized in fearless youth.
I shall forgo actually stepping inside, thank you.

senses: A ball-shaped sweet made with flour and sugar, popular in the Indian subcontinent.
ety: From Hindi लड्डू (laḍḍū).
examples: His foster-mother Yashoda caught him stealing laddus.

senses: The degree of how virulent a thing is.
ety: From Middle French virulence, from Late Latin virulentia.
examples: This strain has higher virulence than most others.

senses: A substance added in small amounts to a pure material, such as semiconductor, to alter its original electrical or optical properties; a doping agent.
ety: From dope + -ant.
examples: It should be noted that even though both types of disorder can be annealed at temperatures well below those where diffusion of the dopant species occurs, there are still defects present.

senses: An elliptical function, equation, path, etc.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”). By surface analysis, ellipse + -tic.
examples: The fix points of hyperbolics and parabolics in F must lie on the fixed circle C, while the fixed points of elliptics in F are inverse with respect to C.

senses: Someone who peeps; a spy.
A peeping tom.
An animal, such as some frogs, having a shrill, high-pitched call.
A chicken just breaking the shell; a young bird.
ety: From peep + -er.
examples: Who's there? peepers, intelligencers, eavesdroppers?

senses: Coarsely, vulgarly, or lewdly amusing; referring to sexual matters in a rude or irreverent way.
ety: From Middle English ribald, from Old French ribaud, ribauld (“rogue, scoundrel”) ( > English ribaud), from Old French riber (“to be licentious”), from Frankish *rīban (“to copulate, be in heat”, literally “to rub”), from Proto-Germanic *wrībaną (“to turn, twist, writhe”), from Proto-Indo-European *werp-, *werb- (“to turn, twist”) + Old French -aud, from Frankish *-wald. Related to Old High German rīban (“to rub”), German reiben (“to rub”), Dutch wrijven (“to rub”). Compare also Old High German hrība (“prostitute”). See also English wrap.
examples: But when he died the "Reform Democracy" instinctively returned to its vomit of ribald insult.

Anyway up against Reba McEntire, '60s-rock-bred big city escapee K.T. Oslin comes off both more ribald ("Younger Men") and prouder of the bras and bridges she used to burn ("'8s Ladies") in her best country hits.
Baron Cohen turns his attentions back towards England, satirising the Establishment’s contempt for what Nobby himself proudly calls “scum” with ribald and corrosive glee.

senses: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).
ety: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).
examples: I took a deep breath; a locomotive howled across-the darkness, Mobile-bound. So were we. I took off my shirt and exulted.

senses: Executed in the manner of a master; showing competence and skill; masterful.
ety: From Middle English maisterli, from maister (“leader, ruler; high official; official in charge of a place; person in control; employer; owner; schoolmaster, teacher; scholar, sage; holder of a master's degree; religious teacher; master craftsman; expert; magician; social superior; husband; lover; Jesus Christ; a god; male stud animal”) + -li (suffix forming adjectives). Maister is derived from Old English mæġester (“master”) and Old French maistre (“master”) (modern French maître), both from Latin magister (“teacher; master”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (“big, great”). The Eng
examples: Her years of experience enabled her to render a masterly performance.
I could not but highly plume myself on my masterly management in getting rid of Bartleby. Masterly I call it, and such it must appear to any dispassionate thinker.
This is a masterly work of condensation, omitting nothing of importance and providing a most readable book that for a modest half-crown is incredibly good value.

senses: A biologist whose speciality is microbiology.
ety: From micro- + biologist.
examples: No, because we obsessively clean it (or use paper coverings at work), said microbiologist Charles Gerba, a professor of public health, environmental science and immunology at the University of Arizona.

senses: Someone who keeps or upholds something; a steward.
A person who does maintenance work.
ety: From Anglo-Norman maintenour, Old French mainteneor, from maintenir (“to maintain”); with later remodelling of the suffix after -er. By surface analysis, maintain + -er.
examples: He become the maintainer of the software project.
RAIB looked at why the washers were missing. This took it into the relationship between the wagon's owner and maintainers.
Muehlendorf told CNN that O’Hara was a crew chief by trade, explaining that his “military occupational specialty was a 15T and he was originally trained to be a maintainer of Black Hawk helicopters.”

senses: A 20th-century philosophical movement emphasizing the uniqueness of each human existence in freely making its self-defining choices; also (generally), a philosophy which emphasizes existence over essence.
The philosophical views of a particular thinker associated with the existentialist movement.
ety: From existential + -ism (suffix forming the names of schools of thought, systems, or theories), modelled after German Existentialismus. The word was popularized by the French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre (1905–1980) in his work L’existentialisme est un humanisme (Existentialism is a Humanism, 1946).
examples: The heyday of existentialism occurred in the mid-twentieth century.
Sartre’s existentialism is atheistic, but the existentialism of Marcel is distinctly Christian.

senses: A member of the community of Internet users.
ety: Blend of Net (“Internet”) + citizen.
examples: The netizen posted their question on the forum.
Do we have to learn a new kind of language — ‘Netspeak’, as I shall call it — in order to be a netizen?
It appeared by Wednesday evening that Congress would follow Bank of America, Netflix and Verizon as the latest institution to change course in the face of a netizen revolt.

senses: A time when conditions are right for the accomplishment of a crucial action; the opportune and decisive moment.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek καιρός (kairós).
examples: The—so-called! friends—rational world. If only they, Mom&Dad&Buddy&Sis, dear-but-square ones, could but know the kairos, the supreme moment…
Kairos is not measurable. Kairos is ontological. In kairos we are, we are fully in isness, not negatively, as Sartre saw the isness of the oak tree, but fully, wholly, positively.

senses: The disposition of the parts of any composition with regard to one another and the whole.
ety: Borrowed from French ordonnance. Doublet of ordinance and ordnance.
examples: August 15, 1833, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Table Talk their dramatic ordonnance of the parts

senses: Equipment or supplies, especially military ones.
A type of horse-drawn carriage.
The carriage together with attendants; a retinue.
ety: From Middle French equippage, from equipper. The "carriage" sense may be influenced by Latin equus (“horse”).
examples: Miserable and desponding he returned to his home; while Oriana, in again taking leave of her family, was borne back in her aunt's equipage to the splendours of the Park.

senses: One who, or that which, persuades, literally or figuratively.
A tool used to pack the type into the form.
An electrode that directs electrons into a multiplier.
ety: From persuade + -er.
examples: Next fit the quoins, using the “persuader” to squeeze in the pages, and tap up all around.
These electrons are guided to the second dynode by the resultant electric field of this dynode and the persuader.

senses: A fur hat, usually with a plume in the front, worn by certain members of the military or brass bands.
ety: Various theories; probably from the surname Busby.
examples: His head was shaped like a busby, a high solid arrogant rock, covered with thick moss.

senses: To remove the cerebrum in order to eliminate brain function.
ety: From de- + cerebrate.
examples: This conceptual experiment can be physically demonstrated by decerebrating or spinalizing an animal and using a neuromuscular blockade or deafferentiation to remove rhythmic sensory feedback.

senses: A gullible fool, especially an elderly person with impaired faculties.
ety: 15th century. From dote (“to be foolish; senile”) + -rel (“pejorative suffix”). The bird is so named as it is easy to catch.
examples: This poor dotterel, Sir Arthur, is playing fast and loose with me.

senses: An auxiliary or accessory.
ety: From Latin ancilla (“maid, slave-girl”).
examples: The filter achieves this two-qubit filtering effect by using two ancilla photons as probes that detect whether or not the two input photons are in the desired states.

senses: A bumper car in an amusement park.
ety: From dodge 'em (“them”).
examples: What better way to let off a little steam, than by zipping around on the dodgems, or flying high on the Cosmic Typhoon roller coaster?

senses: That which is ceded.
A risk, or part of one, which is transferred from one actor to another.
The giving up of rights, property etc. which one is entitled to.
ety: From Middle French cession, from Latin cessionem, from past participle of cēdere (“to yield”). By surface analysis, cede + -sion.
examples: The reinsurance company accepted a 25% cession from the direct insurer.

senses: A bituminous coal that burns brightly with much smoke.
ety: Shortened from cannel coal, corruption of candle coal.
examples: Cannel is dull black in colour while boghead is dull brownish.

senses: A person in whom one can confide or share one's secrets: a friend.
ety: Borrowed from French confident.
examples: One in thought and purpose, linked by the necessity of combating one hostile fate, a power antagonistic ever, — a power we lived to evade, — we had no confidants save ourselves.
Bankman-Fried’s confidants were along for the ride. At his side was Caroline Ellison, Alameda’s CEO and his on-again, off-again lover.

senses: A barber, one whose occupation is to shave.
A tool or machine for shaving; an electric razor.
One who fleeces; a pillager; a plunderer.
A boy; a lad; a little fellow.
ety: From Middle English schaver; equivalent to shave + -er. In its meaning of a boy, lad, recorded since 1592, the word shaver has also been postulated to derive from Romani chavo (“young man”), which also gives us the modern slang chav, ultimately derived from Sanskrit छा (chā, “young animal”).
examples: By these shavers the Turks were stripped.

senses: That removes hair
ety: From French dépilatoire.
examples: You can do anything with electrolytic, depilatory creams and a little patience.
